cues.text: A Boy Preacher
Born Giulio Cesare Russo in 1559 at Brindisi, in the Kingdom of Naples, Lawrence showed such precocious oratorical gift.
By Italian Christmas custom, children preached a short homily on the Infant Jesus, and he was already delivering sermons in his native cathedral to visibly moved congregations at only six years old.
A Master of Languages
Orphaned of his father at twelve, Lawrence continued his education in Venice and entered the Capuchin Franciscans at sixteen.
He completed theological studies at the University of Padua, where he displayed an extraordinary gift for languages.

Over his lifetime, he mastered Latin, Greek, Hebrew, Syriac, German, Bohemian, Spanish, and French, in addition to his native Italian, and reportedly committed much of the Hebrew Bible to memory in its original text.
Preacher to Rome's Jewish Community
Ordained in 1582, Lawrence's linguistic mastery, particularly of Hebrew, led Popes Gregory XIII and Clement VIII to appoint him official apostolic preacher.
In this role, his scholarly rigor and personal respect earned him considerable esteem among those he sought to persuade toward Christianity.
Chaplain at the Battle of Stuhlweissenburg
As the Ottoman Empire pressed into Hungary and Austria in the early 1600s, Lawrence served as chaplain to the Imperial Christian army.
At the decisive battle of Stuhlweissenburg in 1601, roughly 18,000 Christian troops faced some 80,000 Ottoman soldiers.
He is credited by many officers present with rallying the army to victory, riding into the fray carrying only a crucifix rather than a weapon.
Diplomat and Missionary Against Heresy
Elected superior general of the Capuchins in 1602, Lawrence traveled extensively on foot across Italy, France, Belgium, Switzerland, and Spain, establishing the order in new territories.
He spent years directly confronting the spread of militant Protestantism in Bohemia, Austria, and Germany through preaching missions that reclaimed numerous converts back to the Catholic faith.
Legacy
Lawrence died at Lisbon in 1619, while engaged in a diplomatic peace mission to the Spanish court on behalf of the people of Naples.
Canonized in 1881, he was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1959 by Pope John XXIII, with the title 'Apostolic Doctor'.

He was only the third Franciscan, after Sts. Anthony of Padua and Bonaventure , to be so honored, in recognition of theological writing and preaching shaped by his extraordinary command of biblical languages.
